title: Government Budgets
objective: After this level you can explain how a government plans its spending.
summary: A budget, once a leather bag, is a government's plan for what it collects and spends. It runs through four overlapping stages: prepare, approve, carry out and audit.

cards.headline: In 1733, a pamphlet mocked Britain's top minister for opening his bag.
cards.body: The pamphlet was called The Budget Opened, and it attacked Robert Walpole's tax plans, likening him to a quack selling cures. The insult stuck. By the 1760s, 'budget' was simply the word for a government's money plans.

cards.headline: A plan in a bag
cards.body: The word comes from Old French bougette, a small leather bag: picture a finance minister opening his wallet to reveal his plans. Britain's chancellor still holds up a red box on Budget Day. Inside is a plan with two sides: the money the government expects to collect, much of it Level 6's compulsory taxes, and the money it intends to spend over the coming year.

events.label: The executive, the government of the day, puts the plan together
The legislature debates it, amends it and votes on it
The government collects the money and spends it
Auditors check what was actually spent, and whether it worked

mascot.line: Hold on to these four stages; later levels in this chapter keep coming back to them.

cards.fact: At any moment, a government is juggling three budgets at once.
cards.context: While the executive prepares next year's budget, ministries are carrying out this year's, and the national audit office is checking last year's. It works like a school year: next year's timetable gets planned while this year's classes run and last year's exams are still being marked.

cards.headline: Budgets: planned
learned: 'Budget' began as a small leather bag
A budget sets out what's collected and spent
Three budgets are in play at any moment

questions.prompt: The word "budget" comes from an Old French word for what?

options.label: A royal treasury
options.rationale: Close in spirit, but the word meant something you could carry.

options.label: A counting table
options.rationale: That's closer to the root of 'exchequer'; budget was a bag.

options.label: A sealed letter
options.rationale: Letters were sealed; budgets were carried in a bag.

questions.explanation: Budget comes from Old French bougette, a small leather bag, pictured as the minister's wallet of plans.

questions.prompt: While a finance ministry drafts next year's budget, what is usually happening to last year's budget?

options.label: Auditors are checking how it was actually spent
It is being debated for the first time
options.rationale: Debate happens before a budget is carried out, not after.

options.label: It is thrown away and forgotten
options.rationale: Last year's budget still has to be audited.

options.label: It is being spent all over again
options.rationale: Money is spent once, in the year the budget covers.

questions.explanation: Budget cycles overlap: next year's is prepared while this year's is carried out and last year's is audited.

questions.prompt: Level 6 said taxes are compulsory and unrequited. Where do they sit in a government budget?

options.label: On the spending side, as a gift to taxpayers
options.rationale: Taxes are money coming in, not going out.

options.label: On the collecting side, not tied to any one service
Outside the budget, in a separate account
options.rationale: The budget covers what the government collects, taxes included.

options.label: On the audit side, as a fine
options.rationale: Audit checks spending; taxes aren't fines.

questions.explanation: A budget sets out what a government collects and spends. Taxes are on the collecting side, and being unrequited they don't buy any one thing.
